verdict.reasoning: Patient describes “loads of it… super watery… just pouring straight from my bum” and states “it’s been about three days now,” supporting profuse watery diarrhea for 3 days.

Patient reports crampy tummy pain: “I feel, I feel a cramp… around every hour,” located “at the bottom… it feels pretty like in the middle, to me. Not on any side, left or right,” and intermittent: “it comes and goes.” Pain severity: “maybe is that like a six, or a seven?”

Patient says “I definitely feel kind of nauseous… I’ve have vomited,” and “one time I just like had some milk, and I just completely vomited it,” confirming nausea and vomiting with an episode after milk.

Patient reports “I think I am pretty, I feel kind of really hot all the time… I’m pretty sure I’m burning up… I haven’t actually done any temperature reading,” indicating subjective fever without measured temperature.
In response to urine question, patient says “yeah a bit, I guess less frequently maybe. Um but yeah, it seems to be OK,” supporting decreased frequency of urination.

Patient states “my brother has had actually had something like this… for five days, as well” and later “He… he’s been like this for five days. I think he’s getting better, but I’m not really sure,” supporting a similar 5‑day illness and that he is improving.

When asked about medical history, patient says “yeah I think, I think otherwise I’m fit and well… I can’t think of any related medical history… no I don’t think so,” indicating no significant past medical history.
Regarding medications, patient says “I’ve been taking some like Paracetamols and stuff like that lately. But… I’m not on any regular medication,” indicating as‑needed Paracetamol use.
On allergies, patient says “I don’t have any allergies that I know of,” which corresponds to no known allergies.
Patient reports “my dad actually has um colon cancer at the moment… he’s sort of in his third stage,” supporting that father has stage 3 colon cancer.
Home situation: “I live with my, um sister and my mum.” Work: “I work at an office, um in Central London. Um it’s uh, so I work in government,” matching the statement.
Patient says “I smoke… socially, but not like regularly… normally if it’s a Friday or something like that I might have a cigarette,” supporting occasional smoking mainly on Fridays.

Alcohol: “I might have a beer during the weekdays… On Fridays I have more alcohol… not every week, but maybe I’ll once or twice a month… go out with my friends and drink a lot,” matching occasional weekday drinking and heavy drinking 1–2 times per month.

Doctor concludes: “your symptoms are suggestive of something called gastroenteritis… a basic infection of your tummy.” Symptoms discussed include 3 days of watery diarrhea, intermittent midline lower abdominal crampy pain, nausea/vomiting, and subjective feeling of being “really hot… burning up,” consistent with infectious acute gastroenteritis with subjective fevers.

High stool frequency: patient reports going “almost every hour.” Decreased urine: “yeah a bit, I guess less frequently maybe.” Doctor says “you’re losing a lot of fluid there” and later “if you are getting dehydrated then we need to do further investigations,” supporting concern for dehydration risk due to stool and urine changes.

Doctor advises “make sure you drink plenty of fluids” and specifically “you can get things like Diarolyte… a fluid replacement you can get from the pharmacy… no, you can just get that over the counter,” which matches recommending oral rehydration salts like Dioralyte and encouraging clear fluids.

When asked about food, doctor says “clear fluids. You can use soft diet, things like soup, mash. And then gradually build up, um as much as your body can tolerate,” matching the described dietary advice.

Doctor states “you can try just you know regular Paracetamol if you are feeling feverish” and later “If you are having, if you’ve got a bit of tummy pain, if you’re feeling feverish, then I think Paracetamol is very sensible,” supporting as‑needed Paracetamol for fever and abdominal pain.
Doctor clearly advises “Try and avoid alcohol if you can,” matching the statement.

Follow‑up instructions: “if your symptoms aren’t settling down in the next couple of days, so forty eight hours, I want you to give me a call back… if you are getting dehydrated then we need to do further investigations,” supporting the fact about calling back in 48 hours or with signs of dehydration.
